newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast, banks still far apart on debt buyback.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast, banks still far apart on debt buyback.

text.p: Ivory Coast Finance Minister N'Goran Niamien said commercial banks proposed a debt buyback at 41 cents to the dollar as part of a restructuring package for its $6 billion London Club debt.

But Niamien said in an interview shown on Ivorian television on Sunday night that his country made a counter proposal of 15 cents to the dollar. Negotiations were suspended early this month when the two sides failed to reach common ground.
"Ivory Coast's commercial debt on the market today is at 22 cents," Niamien said. "So the commercial banks estimate that the minimum to be considered in terms of negotiation is 22 cents," he said.
"They asked to be paid at the level of 41 cents. We have proposed 15 cents and 15 cents, really, is stretching ourselves," he said.
Official sources said earlier that the banks had lowered their buyback proposal to around 35 cents, but Niamen made no reference to this.
The two sides have been negotiating for the past two years and last met some three weeks ago on the sidelines of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund annual assembly.

Niamien told an interviewer just after the talks that his country and the banks had "reached discord" and were suspending negotiation until November. In his latest interview he did not refer to when talks would resume

The two sides are agreed on a Brady-style debt restructuring plan but they are apart on how much the Ivorians should pay back yearly, the amount of Past Due Interest (PDI) to be converted into Brady bonds and the price and proportion of the buyback portion of the package, bankers say.
Namien has not disclosed the latest figure for how much the banks want Ivory Coast to pay yearly but banking and official sources put this at between 75 billion CFA and 200 billion CFA francs.

An official source told Reuters in July that Ivory Coast had offered at talks in Paris in June to pay 128 billion CFA in 1996 and about 11 billion CFA yearly up to 2000. Its package works out to an average yearly repayment of 21.7 billion CFA between 1997 and 2010.

More than half the Ivorian commercial debt is in form of interest arrears and banking sources close to the talks said the banks want to roll just over $2 billion into Brady bonds. Ivory Coast says it can only afford $730 million, they said.
Niamen stressed in the television interview that the talks had not been ruptured.
"We have hope that we'll reach a solution. We'll pursue negotiations," he said, adding: "There is no point reaching an accord that Ivory Coast cannot respect."
Ivory Coast previously signed a deal with its commercial bank creditors in 1985/86 but has not been able to service this since 1987 because of diminished revenue from cocoa and coffee.
Ivory Coast says it is now a victim of its own economic success: creditors think it can repay debts at any cost simply because of a rebound in its economy.
